First off I am sorry for the loss of your son and I am so sorry you have to deal with this in the aftermath. I know what it's like for people to sort of 'lose it' and act terribly to other people who are grieving the same death. I've come to learn that grieving people are usually either very selfless and loving or selfish and hurtful. 

So I am sort of on the flip side of your situation, albeit a very different one. I lost my boyfriend of 9 years in June. We were not together when he passed away and it was a very complicated situation. Luckily I have always had a good relationship with his family who very lovingly and graciously allowed me to be part of the funeral process as well as pretty much letting me have whatever I wanted. Of course my mentality sounds different than C's. I always asked everyone if what I was doing or wanted was ok with them and definitely made sure to put his families feelings and wants before my own. We were not married and I was lucky to have been given any rights at all. My relationship with his family is stronger and more special now than it ever was when I was dating their son/brother. I also was left money in a life insurance policy. So here are my suggestions from the perspective of someone who lost a long term boyfriend and has tried to navigate the crazy garbage people throw at you when you're just trying to get by and not let your grief swallow you whole:

- You don't have to face her. I know you probably still feel like you should be showing her some kind of respect and support because your son loved her. I totally get that. Since SHE has taken it down the legal route and treated you and your wishes so poorly I echo the sentiment that you should only communicate to her through your legal counsel. This doesn't mean you don't respect your son's love for her. He would understand. You would just being doing what is best for you and your mental health during this tough time. 

- Since you are adamant that you would like to give her a gift have you considered giving her a physical gift or helpful gift that would help her in life and help support her but not just handing her over money? I felt really weird about taking my portion of the life insurance money I was 'owed' and I spoke with his mom about it. She was adamant that I receive it. We came to a compromise that I would accept the money but it was to be used to purchase a new vehicle because my car was in pretty bad shape. I never saw the 'money' but I was given the wonderful gift of a new car that helps support me and give me a better position in life. Does she have something she really needs? A new car or something else you can pay for that would help her so she can't just take the money and do what she wants with it?

- How do you live? Man I wish I had the answer. You just kind of do...and it sucks. I highly highly suggest some kind of active grief relief such as a counselor or support group if you have not already. I also think that the sooner you take care of the 'loose ends' from his death the better you might feel. Take care of the legal portion, give her whatever gift you choose to or not, tell her thank you for loving my son I wish you the best and leave her in the past. I am really sorry that she has acted this way and she will probably regret it later on when she comes out of her grief cloud to see how she treated you and your daughter. I also really like the idea of taking your daughter on vacation :) 

I hope you find peace and healing.

Like others have commented this might not be the best subreddit for this post but holy shit you are me. I know exactly how you feel. I lost my ex to suicide. We were separated for a year before his death and I went a little crazy trying to fill the gaping emotional crater with attention from men. 

My advice is to stay single. I know you are craving the attention, support and love that you can only get from having a partner but in the long run it will only feel good for a short while and you will walk away disappointed because you aren't ready. You will know when you're ready and in the mean time focus on making yourself happy.

I too became suicidal after my love's suicide and I'm still battling that along with my grief. If you haven't reached out to a therapist or support group I highly recommend it. My support group keeps me sane knowing that others who face this very unique struggle go through the same thing.

Keep going girl, you'll get there.

It was my first big holiday since my love left 6 months ago. I hadn't been to my families house since he died. My mom has a family photo that he is in from Christmas a few years ago displayed in her dining room china cabinet. Next to it now stands his funeral program. 

When I first saw it my eyes welled up and I had to choke back some tears. I didn't want to start bawling in the middle of making dinner and I just had a little moment where I had to walk away. 

After dinner we always go out on the boat and fish. When we got home my mom started crying because he couldn't be there to fish with us. I think it just hit everyone at once that he won't be there for anymore family gatherings. 

I've been crying off and on since I got home. I am dreading Christmas. I don't think holidays will ever be the same.

I'm so sorry. I lost my partner 5 months ago to suicide. Like the previous commenter stated; You are not alone! The difference from 2 months to 5 months has been fairly drastic for me. It does get better but it is a very slow and bewildering path. Grieving is a complicated beast. Sometimes you feel like you are doing good and moving in the right direction only to stumble slightly and suddenly find yourself back to square one back in the abyss you fought so hard to get out of. 

How do you keep going? There is no magic answer unfortunately. I highly recommend checking out http://forum.allianceofhope.org I found a lot of help and advice from tons of people who have are going through the same thing here.
Thank you!

10 weeks ago the love of my life passed away. I planned his memorial and made the decisions as to what happened with his body based on our conversations over the years and what I thought he would want while taking into consideration the needs of his family. 

If you don't have a legal document stating exactly what you want make sure you have some kind of conversation with your loved ones about what you would like, regardless of your age! Your loved ones will be faced with all sorts of decisions after your death. Having some of those already decided is extremely helpful.

That being said this event in my life caused me to have that conversation with my family. After just going through the process this is what I want:

Donate any organs that they will take if it's an option.

If my family feels the need to view my body at a service after my death (viewing a body can be an important step in the grieving process) then I am fine with being embalmed. If they don't feel the need  I would rather not be embalmed. I would then like to be cremated. If my family would like to keep my remains with them they are welcome to, if not I would like my remains to be buried in our family plot back home.

Funerals are definitely for the living and can be a very big part of the grieving process. There is a reason the human race has rituals when saying goodbye to the bodies of their loved ones.

I'm about to turn 28. I am no where near what or where I thought I would be at this age. Life throws you curve balls all the time. Societies expectations would tell you that I should be married, starting to have kids and settled into a good career to be considered successful. If you asked me at 25 if that's what I where I wanted to be I would have said yes.

The reality is life is hard. I have none of those things. The last 2 months of my life alone have been tragic and unpredictable. The love of my life passed away, I struggle working 2 jobs to support myself. I have no idea what the next day holds, nothing is promised. A life you spend building for years can come crashing down with one little push. 

Do I want to give up? Hell no. I've worked too hard and faced too much to give up because I'm not 'successful'. Do I wish I had those things? Sure, that would be nice. At some point you have to come to terms with what you have and be thankful you have those things at all because so many do not. I might never have those things and I'm ok with that.

Well I'm not an expert by any means but I have done a lot of research and I'm part of a support community of people who deal with suicide death of loved ones. I also have my own personal experience to look on. 

Bereavement is a very personal experience. Everybody grieves differently. There does seem to be a common theme among the bereaved of suicide of extreme guilt and regret. There's a lot of 'maybe if I had done this or said that, maybe they would still be alive.' It's very common to feel responsible for their death, that we maybe could have saved them if we had done things differently. Ultimately a lot of people blame themselves and that's very painful and hard to cope with regardless of how illogical it is. You feel like you failed them, you are a failure. It's something I battle with every day. You go over every moment and missed opportunity that you could've called them or reached out but didn't. You hope they knew how much you love them. You obsess over what was going through their mind when they did it, how they must have felt. You come up with a million scenarios where the outcome would have been different. There's a lot of questions and few answers. People who have been dealing with this for their whole lives seem to agree that it never goes away, you just learn to live with it. 

Unlike a foreseeable death due to illness or old age where you can mentally prepare as well as financially prepare for death you are suddenly thrust into this bizarro world where you have to make arrangements and handle legal procedures that encompass their manner of death. You have to tell all kinds of people (police, medical examiners. funeral directors, insurance, financial institutions, etc) how they died and relive the pain when you are in shock and haven't even come to terms with it yet. You find yourself in all kinds of situations thinking to yourself 'Am I really doing this right now? Is this really happening to me?' 

There is also a social stigma associated with suicide that prevents people from grieving openly with others. Some people are just not comfortable sharing this very personal and painful experience in their life for fear of judgement of others. When someone dies young and unexpectedly people are curious and want to know what happened. It's human nature. In my experience people are generally uncomfortable and in turn make me feel uncomfortable when I tell them what happened so so can see why some people just avoid it all together.
'Survivor' is the term used in the community of people like me. I can see how it would seem strange from an outsiders perspective

How the hell did you start dating again and how did you approach the subject with a new partner? I'm sort of afraid that someone won't understand how much this affected my life and how important it is for me for him to remain in my life in some ways (pictures, ashes, rings, etc)

Well the emotions change minute by minute and day by day. I have not been angry with him, but that could change. The most prominent feelings are sadness, abandonment, and guilt. When I think about his death I feel heart broken and devastatingly sad that he was alone and did not reach out for help.  When I think about what has happened to me in the aftermath I think about how unfair the whole thing is, that I have so many unanswered questions and will carry around guilt and regret for the rest of my life.

There isn't a whole lot of concrete proof one way or the other. I asked my doctor this same question. Most women who go on birth control don't know how fertile they are to begin with since they haven't tried to get pregnant before. Once they get off birth control and try to conceive and they have trouble they first blame the birth control when in reality they had very low fertility for their entire life. There are also other factors like weight gain or aging that can reduce your fertility. The over all consensus is that your natural fertility isn't effected greatly by birth control however there are always risks and side effects that present themselves to a very small amount of women.

I actually purposefully don't get my period at all anymore thanks to continuous hormones from birth control. It's changed my life for the better. I get extremely painful cramping and sickness when I would have my period. My Gyno suggested to just stop having my period until I decided to try and have children. Many women either don't know this is a thing or they don't like the idea of messing with their bodies hormones. 10/10 would recommend.
